reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: RAROC numerator for a USD 2m loan, no taxes or transfers. Gross revenue USD 250,000; interest expense USD 100,000; operating costs USD 60,000; expected loss 300 bp of the loan; return earned on economic capital USD 10,000. Economic capital is USD 400,000.
ask: Risk-adjusted income (the numerator) is closest to:

options.label: USD 30,000
options.why: Left out the USD 10,000 return on economic capital, which is added back: 250,000 - 60,000 - 60,000 - 100,000 = 30,000.

options.label: USD 100,000
options.why: Forgot expected loss: 300 bp of USD 2m is USD 60,000 and it must come off revenue.

options.label: USD 140,000
options.why: Left out the USD 100,000 interest expense on the deposits that fund the loan.

takeaway: RAROC numerator = revenue less funding cost, operating cost and expected loss, plus the return earned on the economic capital.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A EUR 1.5m loan is funded by deposits. Expected revenue EUR 52,500 a year; expected loss EUR 20,000; direct operating costs EUR 15,000. Economic capital of EUR 90,000 earns a risk-free 2%. Tax rate 30%; no transfers.

options.why: Percent as decimal: 0.1501 read off as if it were already a percentage.
Divided income by the EUR 1.5m loan instead of the EUR 90,000 of economic capital.
Revenue over economic capital: ignores expected loss, operating costs, and tax.

takeaway: RAROC divides by economic capital, not by the loan; the capital here is only 6% of the loan, so the ratio is much larger than the margin on assets.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A CNY 3.8bn one-year loan is funded by deposits. The loan pays 4.1%, deposits cost 0.6%, expected loss is 3.0% of the loan and operating costs 0.3%. Economic capital is 15% of the loan and earns 2%. Tax rate 38%; no transfers.

options.label: Above 5%
options.why: Left out expected loss (3.0% of the loan), which takes almost all of the 3.5% spread; that slip gives about 14%.

takeaway: Check what is left of the spread after expected loss: here it is a sliver, and dividing by 15% capital cannot lift it past 5%.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: Firm QZK's hurdle rate uses CAPM for its common equity. Common equity return volatility is 14%, market volatility 20%, and the correlation between the two is 0.65. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return 8%.
ask: QZK's equity beta is closest to:

options.why: Used the correlation itself as beta; beta also needs the volatility ratio.
Used $\sigma_E/\sigma_M = 14/20$ and forgot to multiply by the correlation.
Inverted the volatility ratio: $0.65 \times 20/14$.

takeaway: Beta is the correlation times the ratio of the stock's volatility to the market's, so it sits below both 0.65 and 0.70 here.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A bank is funded by USD 800m of common equity and USD 200m of preferred equity (market values). Common equity has beta 1.30; the risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return 9%. The preferred dividend yield is 6.0%.
ask: Compared with the CAPM cost of common equity, the bank's hurdle rate is:

options.label: Above it
options.why: Treated the cheaper preferred layer as if it raised the average, or weighted it more than the 20% it represents.

options.label: Equal to it
options.why: Ignored the preferred equity and used the common equity cost alone (10.80%).

takeaway: The hurdle rate is a weighted average of the costs of each capital source, so a cheaper layer pulls it below the common equity cost.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: Adjusted RAROC criterion: accept a project if RAROC $- \beta_E(R_M - R_F) > R_F$. The project has the same beta as Sigma Inc., 1.18. The risk-free rate is 2% and the expected market return is 7.932%.
ask: The systematic charge $\beta_E(R_M - R_F)$ is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied beta by the risk-free rate (1.18 × 2%) instead of by the market premium.
Forgot beta: that is just the market premium 7.932% - 2%.
Added the risk-free rate on top. That is the minimum RAROC for acceptance, a later step.

takeaway: The charge scales the market premium by beta; the risk-free rate is added only when setting the hurdle for RAROC.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A project has RAROC 13%. The risk-free rate is 6%, the market return 14%, the firm's equity beta 1.5, and the firm's required return on equity 12%. The rule: accept if adjusted RAROC, RAROC $- \beta_E(R_M - R_F)$, exceeds the risk-free rate.

options.label: Accepted: 13% beats the 12% required return
options.why: Compared unadjusted RAROC with the required return. The rule uses adjusted RAROC against the risk-free rate; 12% plays no part.

options.label: Rejected: adjusted RAROC is below the risk-free rate

takeaway: Adjusted RAROC is compared with the risk-free rate; the charge for market risk can wipe out most of a headline RAROC.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Three derivatives with one counterparty sit under an enforceable bilateral netting agreement (EUR m): an interest rate swap worth +95, an FX forward worth -35 and a stock option worth +80. The 1995 Amendment defines the net replacement ratio as net current exposure divided by gross current exposure (positive values only).

options.label: Above 1
options.why: Divided gross by net, so the ratio came out the wrong way up (175/140 = 1.25).

options.label: Exactly 1
options.why: Ignored the negative FX forward; it offsets under netting but is floored at zero in the gross figure.

takeaway: Netting can only reduce exposure, so NRR is at most 1; it falls as negative values offset positive ones.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Two counterparties, each with its own enforceable netting agreement (USD m market values). Counterparty 1: interest rate +20, interest rate 0, wheat -5. Counterparty 2: equity 0, FX -10. NRR is net exposure divided by gross exposure, where net exposure is the sum over counterparties of $\max(\text{sum of values}, 0)$.

options.why: Netted across both counterparties (20 - 5 - 10 = 5, then 5/20). Netting works only within a counterparty.
Inverted the ratio: gross over net (20/15).

takeaway: A counterparty with a net negative value contributes zero; it cannot offset another counterparty's positive exposure.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II standardised approach. Exposures (USD m) and external-rating risk weights: 24 at 80%, 12 at 120%, 18 at 70%, 17 at 30% and 3 at 10%. Minimum capital is 8% of risk-weighted assets.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.41m
options.why: Used 0.8% instead of 8% (percent slip).

options.label: ≈ USD 52m
options.why: Stopped at risk-weighted assets and never took 8% of them.

options.label: ≈ USD 645m
options.why: Multiplied RWA by 12.5, going back from capital the wrong way.

takeaway: Capital is 8% of RWA, not RWA itself; capital times 12.5 gives RWA back.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II collateral: a USD 100m exposure to a counterparty with 150% risk weight is secured by USD 80m of bonds with 50% risk weight. Simple approach: collateral weight on the covered USD 80m, counterparty weight on the rest. Comprehensive approach: first raise the exposure 10% and cut the collateral 15%; collateral weight applies to the cut collateral, counterparty weight to the remaining exposure.
ask: RWA under the comprehensive approach, compared with the simple approach, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Assumed the comprehensive approach is always the kinder one. Haircuts shrink the collateral credit and grow the uncovered exposure.

options.label: The same
options.why: Ignored the haircuts, so both approaches cover USD 80m at 50%.

takeaway: Haircuts are conservative: less collateral credit and more exposure left uncovered, so comprehensive RWA rises here.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II IRB, retail portfolio (no maturity adjustment). Exposure at default USD 400m, LGD 35%, PD 2% and worst-case default rate at 99.9% of 10%. Capital is EAD $\times$ LGD $\times$ (DR$_{99.9}$ - PD), and RWA is capital $\times$ 12.5.

options.label: ≈ USD 2.8m
options.why: Used PD alone: EAD × LGD × PD is expected loss, not capital, and there was no 12.5.

options.label: ≈ USD 11m
options.why: Stopped at the capital charge (11.2) and never multiplied by 12.5.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,750m
options.why: Dropped the $(DR_{99.9} - PD)$ term: 400 × 0.35 × 12.5.

takeaway: IRB capital is on the unexpected loss only (worst-case minus PD); RWA is that capital scaled up by 12.5.
